glosses: To distribute objects or pieces of something over an area, especially in a random manner.

examples.text: to strew sand over a floor
The files had been strewn all over the floor.
Sweet flower, with flowers thy bridal bed I strew.
And strewed his mangled limbs about the field.

[…] I ſee
Th’ Inſulting Tyrant prancing o’er the Field
Strow’d with Rome’s Citizens, and drench’d in Slaughter,
His Horſe’s Hoofs wet with Patrician Blood.
On a principal table a desk was open and many papers strewn about.

glosses: To cover, or lie upon, by having been scattered.

examples.text: Leaves strewed the ground.
The snow which does the top of Pindus strew.
Is thine alone the seed that strews the plain?

glosses: To spread abroad; to disseminate.

examples.text: She may strew dangerous conjectures.

glosses: To populate with at random points; to cause to appear randomly distributed throughout.

examples.text: error-strewn

glosses: Straw, grass, and similar loose material used as bedding for people or animals.

examples.text: Quen he had made me hale and fere

As pelows ben to chambres agreable
 So is harde strawe lytter for the stable.
To place daily under those Animals... a sufficient quantity of fresh New Straw, well spread, which is call'd making of Litter.

The afterwards dry the horsedung in the sun, beat it with a mallet through fine sieves, and make it into litter for the horses; for no straw can be obtained for litter in Constantinople.

glosses: A bed, especially a pile of straw with blankets &c. used as a bed.

examples.text: The traitours sought the Kyng... yn the withdrawyng chaumburs, yn the litters, undir the presses.

glosses: A mobile bed or couch transported upon or suspended from poles placed over human shoulders or animal backs.

examples.text: ... In a lytter made tho full royall...

 And driue toward Douer friend...

glosses: A mobile bed or couch transported upon or suspended from poles placed over human shoulders or animal backs.
Synonym of stretcher, such a vehicle used for transporting the sick and injured, inclusive of designs carried in the hand.

examples.text: He ordeyned lyttyers for the wounded knyghtes.

glosses: A mobile bed or couch transported upon or suspended from poles placed over human shoulders or animal backs.
The general category of all such similar vehicles, inclusive of sedan chairs, hammock litters, and the like.

examples.text: When they went out, they sat in litters, which were curtained.

"The Chengtu revolutionaries were fantastically colourful in the Szechwanese manner—they costumed themselves as heroes of the stage and their energies were chiefly occupied in tying ropes across the main streets so that when Imperial officials rode by in their litters they would have to get down and crawl under, losing face.

glosses: An act of giving birth to a number of live young at the same time.
Synonym of straw, grass, &c. more generally, particularly in plaster, thatch, and mulch.

examples.text: Let new planted Elms be kept moist by frequent refreſhings upon ſome half-rotten Fern, or Litter laid about the foot of the ſtem...

glosses: The whole group of live young born at the same time, typically in reference to mammals or (figurative, derogatory) unpleasant people or objects.

examples.text: A Wolf came to a Sow, and very Kindly Offer'd to take care of her Litter.
Strongly-marked differences occasionally appear in the young of the same litter.
When a man had married into a family where there was a whole litter of women, he might have plenty to put up with if he choose.
The runt of the litter is the smallest or weakest of a group of puppies born together.

glosses: Waste or debris, originally any mess but now particularly trash left or thrown on the ground.

examples.text: What are you doing?! There's a litter bin not three feet away.

Strephon, who found the room was void
 And Betty otherwise employed,
 Stole in and took a strict survey
 Of all the litter as it lay....
The British people seem incapable of avoiding the habit of leaving litter wherever they go, and the railways certainly seem to receive their fair share of it, in carriages and on stations.

In the case of a simple problem such as littering, the success or failure of a solution can immediately be assessed once and for all. A successful solution is one that results in no litter being present. Assuming the solution did not involve summarily executing anyone suspected of being about to drop litter, it is unlikely to have significant second-order effects.

glosses: Animal bedding together with its dung.

examples.text: Silkworms... must be well cleansed from the litter.

The heir of an estate... troubled himself little about decorating his abode, and, if he attempted decoration, seldom produced anything but deformity. The litter of a farmyard gathered under the windows of his bedchamber, and the cabbages and gooseberry bushes grew close to his hall door.

glosses: A bed, a substrate formed from loose materials.

examples.text: Having first made a litter of shingles, planks or billets, with a layer of charcoal powder several inches in thickness...

glosses: The layer of fallen leaves and other loose organic material on the ground in a forest.

examples.text: Litter, that portion of the forest floor which is not in an advanced state of decomposition.
Forest animals use leaf litter in a variety of ways, including as food, shelter, nesting material, bedding, and camouflage.

glosses: Fuller's earth, clay pellets, wood chips, or other similar loose absorbent materials used for the waste of pet animals.

examples.text: Change the cat litter fer chrissakes. This place reeks.

glosses: To drop or throw trash without properly disposing of it (as discarding in public areas rather than trash receptacles).

examples.text: By tossing the bottle out the window, he was littering.

glosses: To scatter carelessly about.
To strew (a place) with scattered articles.

examples.text: Their Clamour, 'lighting from their Chairs, / Grew lowder, all the way up Stairs; / At Entrance louder, where they found, / The Room with Volumes litter'd round; [...]

glosses: To give birth to, in the manner of animals.

examples.text: We might conceive that dogs were created blind, because we observe they were littered so with us.
The son that she did litter here, / A freckled whelp hagborn.

glosses: To produce a litter of young.

examples.text: A desert […] where the she-wolf still littered.

glosses: To supply (cattle etc.) with litter; to cover with litter, as the floor of a stall.

examples.text: Tell them how they litter their jades.
For his ease, well litter'd was the floor.

glosses: To be supplied with litter as bedding; to sleep or make one's bed in litter.

examples.text: The inn where he and his horse litter'd.

glosses: comparative form of lit: more lit

A group of such animals, also of locomotives.

examples.text: He had the finest stud in England, and his delight was to win plates from Tories.

glosses: An animal (usually livestock) that has been registered and is retained for breeding.
A place, such as a ranch, where such animals are kept.

examples.text: In the studs of persons of quality in Ireland, where care is taken, […]we see horses bred of excellent shape, vigour, and size.
